sent_emails.subject: Re: Negative NDRE Re: Annual Review — Wooldridge Carbon Projects
sent_emails.body: Good Morning Andrew, Glad to hear that you are getting there. This graph shows NDRE not the carbon prediction for your farm. NDRE basically measures how green plants are and how much area has green plants across time on the project. The satellite takes a reading each day to make this graph. We use this as an indicator of if carbon sequestration has been likely. So this is showing greenness and not carbon exactly. Looking at your graph that is a very extreme drop, so I am going to check in with the tech team to make sure that there is nothing data related doing this, but if you look back across the graph it does seem like August in other years has had a downward trend and so could've been a tough time on your farm with less green feed each year. Generally, the dips will be a combination of seasonal changes and grazing, or if you have crops when there are big areas in fallow or very small crops there is obviously less green on the areas overall and this line would go down. Do you remember after your baseline having a pretty tough dry time? (probably around 4 months or so) The other thing it could be (which we will look into on our end ) is if its cloudy or its snowing the satellite cannot take a reading so will mark that day as a 0 value - this graph shows the rolling average - so if there is a very cloudy period it could have logged months of 0's which put your average right down and fast and then the days since then have been helping it come back up as they are actual values, but starting lower because that lack of data dragged the average down. This would make sense also for what this graph looks like. We will look into it. I had a bit of play around and looked at our model and what the result with that drop excluded would've been and things are looking good. Carbon Project 1 is indicating a very slight increase and Carbon Project 2 is showing potentially around an 800tC increase which would indicate that next year once the carbon effects of the fire has had some time to pass you would likely be able to apply for credits after confirming with samples. Please note these values on our model are still in testing so will not be 100% accurate, but are showing that things are going well despite this NDRE graph result. If we find any issues we will be able to note this so that we don take this weird data into consideration in your next annual review. Any questions feel free to give me a call, Kind Regards, Claudia Claudia Bryant | Customer Success Specialist Phone: 1300467465 Mobile: +61483969401 Email: claudia@agriprove.io Address: Level 1, 601 Dean Street Albury NSW 2640 Here at AgriProve we care for your privacy. sent_emails.subject: Re: Horizon
sent_emails.body: Hey Alec, No Worries. It's always good to check in case there is something wrong. Great to hear it's all going well! The HORIZON map is showing the carbon level change predictions for your farm. It uses all different layers and satellite imagery to get a prediction of what the carbon has done overtime. So the model does a prediction of how much carbon has increased or decreased across your farm since baseline (say for each 30m square - I dont know the exact area) and then it groups it together to make the map you're seeing. So instead of you seeing all the little squares it smooths it out into areas to show you the lowest performing areas in orange, the areas that are within the average range in green and the highest performing areas in dark green. This makes it easier to action as it looks smoother and less complicated but does remove some of the finer details between areas in those zones. These are though just showing the relative areas on your farm- so where the best performance is in terms of carbon change is, it doesn't indicate if its an increase or decrease e.g. a farm that's in drought and has had a decrease will still have all 3 colours and in that case the dark green would in theory show where they lost the least. ( it shows you the highest performing in terms of carbon but we don't currently indicate in platform if that is an increase or by how much). So ultimately the model measures carbon change using satellite imagery, The current HORIZON map shows you your best performing areas, and the next step is for us to show the actual carbon predictions in the platform. It does this maths already we just aren't confident showing it publicly to everyone in the platform until we have done some more testing and are confident that the predictions are accurate as the model is pretty new.) sent_emails.subject: Re: Horizon
sent_emails.body: Hi Alec, Thanks for your feedback. We are planning to build in being able to see it overtime and we are planning to also have it so that you can see it at a finer detail than what you can now e.g. more than just the 3 zones you can currently see. We will send out an email when the updates are finished. I have checked in on this for you. The tech team said that when a project doesn't have a lot of variation it will show as all green. They do this as each project shows the 3 zones (below average, average and high performing) for each project area, so If you could see the same 3 zones in the projects that are fairly consistent throughout next to other projects that have more variation it would appear like there was more areas to prioritise that are not actually outliers. E.g. The orange in a consistent area would NOT be much different from the green in those consistent areas, whereas orange or dark green in the more variable areas could be significantly lower or higher performing than the rest of the project and a better place to prioritise and use for decision making. What this means for your project is that the carbon stocks are fairly consistent and uniform across the area of the project that is all green and so there is less variation and therefore the zones are no longer showing. This doesn't mean something big changed on ground - it means that most of this area is performing at a similar level and there is no large or extreme under or overperforming areas in that project. Why you could see it before and can't now is that the threshold for variation to be seen is 5% and your project in the January run just ticked over that 5. Then every other month since then it has been under the threshold and would be seen as all green ( see attached graph). "I have checked with the operations team to check on their eligibility and Will said the below: The olive grove can be considered eligible land as cropping is a land use. Then - in regards to clearing: (2) Woody vegetation may be cleared only if: (a) any clearing is undertaken in accordance with any applicable regional natural resource management plan and Commonwealth, State, Territory or local government environmental and planning laws; and (b) at least one of the following apply: (i) the clearing is to manage woody horticulture crops, as part of standard business operations; (ii) the clearing is required to manage woody horticulture crop, following a disturbance; (iii) the clearing is to manage growth of a known weed species as defined in the CFI Regulations; (iv) the clearing is required to reduce the risk of fire; (v) the land was not forest cover in the 5 years prior to the lodgement of the section 22 application for the project or the section 29 application for the land. sent_emails.subject: HORIZON Model Check in
sent_emails.body: Good Morning Noel, Thanks for your time on the phone yesterday. It was good to chat to you again. I have looked into your query about the HORIZON model. As I mentioned on the phone the HORIZON model is currently predicting a decrease of 500 t of carbon. This seems unusual due to you having a positive lead indicator last year, a good season, HORIZON layer showing mostly strength on your platform map and you have seen improvements in your soil tests. In looking into it - the model is noting a very low confidence in this prediction. This could be due to the small size of the project, location or potentially it just not having enough data points in your area. The team are going to look into this a bit more deeply to see if they can narrow down exactly why this might be and make a plan of attack going forwards. At this stage the intention is to still go ahead and put you in the schedule 2 group as discussed. Once they figure out what the reason for unusual result is they may decide to resample your project as normal this time - which should then give the model more calibration to be accurate going forwards or anywhere in between depending on the cause. The groups aren't expected to start running till June so just a heads up that you may not hear a confirmed answer on this till at least then depending on which group you fall in. E.g. If you are in group 2 it may be even later than June before they lock in the plan. I will keep checking in on this for you. Know it is moving and we are going to look into finding whatever solution works best for your project. If you have any questions- feel free to give me a call anytime. I have not forgotten this task…regards Ross From: Claudia Bryant Sent: Wednesday, 25 February 2026 1:16 PM To: Ross Thompson Cc: Imogen Hickey Subject: Carbon Project Records Good Morning Ross, Thanks for your time on the phone today. It was nice to meet you. I have checked in on a few things for you and put together a list of what we need for your 5-year reporting below. One thing I also forgot to mention is that we can do a lot of math and working through the details for you once we have the paperwork, so don't feel like you have to do everything right now. We can get the paperwork, see what we have, and ask you any questions to fill in the gaps as we work through the report. Information to pull together: 1. A map of the areas of fencing at the start of the project and then what it looks like now. (Daley and Chifley can be on the same map if that is easiest) 1. Simple list of the 4 properties with their sizes, label and when you started leasing or bought. E.g. Tonys, 500ha, March 2017-now 1. Livestock numbers from accountant: the best way to prove your numbers is getting your accountant to write out a table with your livestock inventory numbers for the past 10 years in their format, e.g. letter head. That way it saves you some time, looks official and is a document we can attach as evidence of your livestock numbers for the regulator as sometimes they will be a bit wary of farmers' notes being attached alone. 1. Breakdown of inventory: once you have those numbers together, an estimate of the breakdown of different livestock classes within those totals is needed. E.g. Bulls, weaners, calves, cows, steers, heifers and weights if you know. If this is getting really hard let us know and we can try work through it together. 1. Another good thing for this is your NLIS records - Even if you haven't been changing them every time between farms- it is a good way to show what came and went from your business in terms of being on your farms and sold. Optional for now, but would be helpful and should be easy to get. 1. Your fertilizer records- you mentioned you have all of your records in a big word document. This is exactly what we need for the emissions calculations around inputs. What you used, when and where. As far back as you can go is helpful. 1. Agriwebb data - anything you have in there around fertilizer, livestock moves or numbers . I think you are able to export out of Agriwebb or are able to give us permissions to view things like they do for agronomists ect. If you need help with this let me know. Once we have this information together, we will be able to narrow down if we need anything extra. For example: we may need receipts for fencing materials, fuel, comments around grazing or similar things to fill in some gaps for auditors, but for now this will get the ball rolling and should be enough to do the majority of the report. sent_emails.body: Good Afternoon Ella, Sorry to hear that things have not been going to plan. I completely understand your uncertainty in continuing with the project. From our end - if you are still committed to making these improvements in the long term, we would encourage you to continue with the project. Poor seasons are something that happens in farming and therefore carbon projects, and that is why the contracts are 25 years long. If you are still interested, there is still an opportunity for you to measure an increase and receive ACCU's in the future when you are able to implement your chosen activities. If you would not like to continue, the main thing you need to know is that there will be a fee to repay the Clean Energy Regulators Advanced Payment that was used at the beginning of your project for the baseline sampling. sent_emails.body: Good Afternoon Henry, Thanks for getting in touch. I have just completed your Annual Review so this is good timing. This means that your project would not normally have met our threshold for resampling. However, as your project has reached the 5-year mark we will need to resample it ASAP. The records we need are: 1. Things showing that since starting the project in the past 5-6 years how stocking rate has changed- So this can be map's showing fencing you have done since starting the project, grazing records showing that you have changed the number of grazing days and rest ect. - these can be in any format that you have them in. We will take whatever you have even if its hand written and will ask questions or refine them if we need. Do you have those sorts of records? 1. For the emissions calculations - we need your fertilizer use from the 5 years of the project and the 5 years before the project started. We also need estimated of your livestock numbers each year for the 5 years of the project and the 5 years before the project. People usually do this from their own records or as a starting point you can get your accountant to write out a document showing your livestock inventory over time. sent_emails.subject: HORIZON Further Information
sent_emails.body: Good Afternoon Jeff, I received your email in the past few weeks with your version of what you thought the HORIZON map should look like. It was very interesting, so thanks for taking the time to pull that together and send it to me. Sorry that it took a while to get back to you - I was getting tech team to pull together some information to pass onto you. Attached to this email is the HORIZON layer, but with more detail than what you will currently see on the platform. On the platform we have smoothed out the areas to make it not so busy and more actionable on farm, but this is better showing what it is actually able to capture. I think it is pretty close to your drawing and does capture a lot of the variation that you had in your drawn map which is good! In regards to your questions - here is some more information about how it works to help you going forwards: 1. You mentioned being concerned with satellite imagery not being able to identify the cycling of forage and its density: The model actually is able to detect this and take this into consideration. The model doesn't currently measure pasture quantity and ground cover specifically as the main determiners of the areas. It has been trained to know what layers/factors eg. Soil type or other factors, and visually what pastures look like from the satellite have led to soil carbon increases and by how much to be able to predict it from the imagery. It is obviously more complicated than this, but the greenness measurements taken from the satellite are key here. A pasture that is tall dry and dormant from a satellite is going to not be green, where as a productive pasture cycles between growing seasons and grazing and it will cycle through greenness levels- giving a stronger indicator of soil carbon sequestration than pasture that is not productive, green and growing across time. For this reason, it doesn't really need to know exactly what that ground cover is exactly e.g. 100% love grass or how dense/pasture quantity necessarily as it can see other things such as greenness and has been trained to know what the most important predictive factors are in soil organic carbon. The model is much smarter and able to detect finer details than we can with our eyes. This means it is very capable of identifying the dieback and where there is anaerobic love grass and ongoing what parts have the best species and diversity that lead to carbon as they will have reflecting data points e.g. multi species has more green across the year, longer seasons ect. The model will tell you where its seeing the best results - its up to us on ground to then identify what's different in those areas and replicate it across farm. Going forwards as we sample your project we will also be able to update the model to specifically understand your property . E.g. It will learn what factors matter on your property and where get the best results to calibrate it more accurately. If you have any further questions or queries, always feel free to get in touch. sent_emails.subject: Carbon Project - Annual Review
sent_emails.body: Good Afternoon Craig, I have just completed the Annual Satellite review of your carbon project. We do these every 12 months using satellite imagery of the NDRE ( Normalized Difference Red Edge) on your farm to get an idea of if the vegetation has indicated that carbon sequestration is likely to have occurred in the past 12 months and we should resample at this time. As you will see in the attached document, your projects average NDRE has had a negative trend when compared to the baseline period. This does not mean that carbon has gone backwards; it means that compared to baseline the average trend has not be positive - which is an indicator that carbon sequestration has been unlikely at this time. sent_emails.subject: Re: Horizon
sent_emails.body: Good Afternoon Alec, Glad to hear you are excited about it. The areas that you see are based on the SOC model predictions, but also its relative within your farm. ( all measured from satellite predictions) So the best areas that are showing are the areas where the SOC model has had the most predicted change in soil carbon since your baseline period or had the most positive indicators present in those areas. It doesn't necessarily mean those areas have had an increase in carbon - its the best within your projects. For example: the people that have been in 3 years of drought and had barely any ground cover will still be seeing all 3 types of zones for their farms, its not showing where you are getting carbon and where you are not. We are planning to show specific predictions of carbon sequestered in the future, but we need to do a bit more testing on how accurate the predictions are before we are comfortable showing them in the platform. This model will be run every month ( see the timer in top right hand corner of the panel showing you when the next update will be ) and it will be updated in the platform automatically no matter the result. On our end if the model ran and predicted a worthwhile increase we are notified and would then look to resample even if it was out of your usual review time. This model allows us to check each month and act when a large enough increase is predicted instead of doing it once a year like we have in the past. IN the platform month to month you may not notice a huge difference as a month is not long in carbon time and therefore It you may take a while to see a large change in the areas that are in this current map layer. We are hoping to get some more time-based information and graphs in there in the future/ Hope you are well and if you have any more questions Im happy to chat. I will be in touch with you when your project has been declared and let you know when its okay for you to begin. sent_emails.subject: Re: Carbon Project - Important Actions
sent_emails.body: Good Morning Hamish, Thanks for getting this information back to me. I will get in touch with your bank manager in the next few weeks to get this moving. Your reporting deadline is not until August, so we do have a bit of time to tick everything off. In terms of the bank needing to give consent - we have to collect it as it's a requirement from the clean energy regulator. My understanding is they collect all eligible interest holder's consent as protection for the project by making sure everyone with an interest is aware of the project and acknowledges their intent to continue to meet its obligations. Eg. If someone involved with land didn't know about the project they may do something against the rules, people may try to sell their property and not mention it, people have tried to run projects without other owners knowing and some types of carbon projects require changes of practice which may impact your ability to pay the mortgage. sent_emails.body: HI Paul, Thanks for that. I will get the forms for you to sign in the next week as Its very simple with no bank. For the records: You have sent 2021 till now which is the current 5 years which is great thankyou. We do though need records for the 5 years before that too (2016-2020). If you didn't own the farm it's simply saying that . Eg. just write down Farm purchased in 2018 ( if they need proof we can get that later), then we need what you did for the first few years before starting the project. If that is not a lot that's okay but we need specifics of what that little bit was. The reason is - the main thing you have to prove to the regulator is that you are doing something NEW/different since starting the project. Your 2x activities are reestablishing and rejuvenating pasture by seeding or pasture cropping and applying fertilizer. We need to show how the fertilizer you have been doing is different to before (eg. rates, forms and types) and what you have done since starting the project with pasture improvement. sent_emails.subject: Carbon Projects Annual Review
sent_emails.body: Good Afternoon Geoff and Mitch, I am getting in touch as I have completed the annual satellite review of your carbon projects. These use satellite NDRE ( Normalized Difference Red Edge) data to get an idea of if the vegetation in the projects has indicated that carbon sequestration is likely to have occurred in the past 12 months and we should resample. As you will see in the attached document: The Watson Carbon Project has had a positive indicator suggesting that resampling would be worthwhile. We have also run this through HORIZON and it has backed that up. This means carbon sequestration is likely, and we are intending to resample this project asap. The Cooper & Beale Projects had a negative trend when compared to the baseline period. This does not mean that carbon has gone backwards; it is an indicator that suggests that the positive change has not been more since baseline and therefore carbon sequestration is unlikely to have occurred. These have not met the threshold for resampling at this time. In the next few months when we have our HORIZON model up and running we will be able to do a regular assessment of these with more factors included which will give us more information and trigger a resampling when it is indicated. sent_emails.subject: Soil Sampling Results
sent_emails.body: Good Morning Peter, Sorry that it took a few days to get back to you. Your soil sampling results have been completed and are attached. As you will see in the results, there has been an increase in your soil carbon levels since your baseline sampling of 115tC. This is a positive result as it indicates that your on-farm activities are working and have resulted in the sequestration of carbon. At present though, this increase is not sufficient to warrant progressing to crediting at this time. From here we will continue to monitor your project using the HORIZON soil carbon model ( which you will be able to view next year in the platform) and re-assess next year if we should sample and apply for credits then. If you would like to get ahead and have things ready for when a sufficient increase is measured, there are some things you can do that will allow crediting to occur faster when the time comes. This includes: 1. Starting to pull together your records of what you have been doing in your project that will be needed for the crediting audit. This is management records since you started your project and the 5 years before starting. 2. You can start the process of applying for unconditional declaration. For more information on this click here to read our knowledge base article. If you have further questions, you can contact Will Frecheville on +61 402 726 315. Have a great Christmas and New year. sent_emails.subject: Follow Up from Carbon Project Call
sent_emails.body: Good Afternoon, Martin, Thanks for your time on the phone last week. I have followed up on some of the things we spoke about. 1. Getting your Map into the Platform Currently you can't enter your own maps of your paddocks, but if you have a map (digital or a decent drawn) we are happy to enter that for you. Ideally this map will have a satellite photo as the base, so it's easy for us to copy, but we can make do with whatever you have. If you send me a map, I can get our team onto doing that for you. 2. Biodiversity Project The main people I know of that do biodiversity projects are Renovo Ag. Their contact details are: simon.campbell@renovoag.com.au , 0409 870 894 3. Potential Carbon Day in your Area As I mentioned, we would love to do some events in your area if you think there is interest. We can tailor it to the audience, e.g. go right back to basics of carbon, specifically talk about projects or do a paddock walk to show others what you are doing and link that to carbon. We are happy to handle the organizing if you are sure there is interest. sent_emails.subject: Carbon Project Record's & Update
sent_emails.body: Good Afternoon Paul, Thanks for your time on the phone today. As discussed, the next steps will be: 1. We are going to vary your start date till after your baseline period - This has no effect on you other than giving us all more time to get the records together for the 5-year deadline. This may also be an advantage as it will push out your sampling to April next year and it may not be as dry as it is now. 2. Early next year we will put your project through our new model to get a better indicator of if carbon sequestration has been likely and look to schedule your 5-year sampling. Our operations team will be in touch when that is done and they are organizing the logistics. ( I expect that to be in February/March). * 3. From Now we will start pulling together all of your records for you to complete the 5-year audit. There are a few steps to this, but as a start we need to get together your management history from before the baseline period and then now the 5 years since the project has started. TO GET STARTED WITH THE RECORDS: What we need to prove is that you have done things differently since commencing the project ( start date 19/01/2021) - focusing on your nutrient application, what you have sown and anything that could have improved carbon like lime, fencing and grazing management. To do this, we basically need WHAT was done, WHEN and WHERE. E.g. 50kg of Urea/ ha was applied to paddock 1 and 2 which is a total of 150 ha and ideally with evidence eg. receipts - the more detail the better as a change can be you used to apply 100kg and now you do 50kg, you used to apply it in 1 form and now you've put it out as something different, you used to sow oats and now you do a mix, you used to do a summer mix and since starting you've put in a winter mix ect. - the practice change doesn't need to be the same across your whole place, but something different does need to be shown across your whole project. So as a starting point: * if you could get together those rudimentary notes about what was done in each paddock over the time since you had the farm ( as detailed as possible like mentioned above) * A paddock map would be great if you have one ( can be simple drawn or photo ) so we can visually understand what has happened where from those notes. Once we have an idea of this - we can make a plan of attack and let you know what specific evidence you need. If you have any questions feel free to give me a call anytime. Each year we complete a review via satellite of your project to see if the NDRE ( Normalized Difference Red Edge) trend on your farm in the past 12 months is indicative of soil carbon sequestration. We compare the recent trend to those of the 5 years prior to baseline sampling. As you will see in the attached document, your projects average NDRE has had a negative trend compared to the baseline period. This means that your project has not met our threshold for us to complete resampling this year. Next year we will review your project again to decide if resampling would be worthwhile. Please note: This trend does not mean carbon has gone backwards, it shows the trend in vegetation greenness has been lower than your baseline average and therefore it is unlikely re sampling would be worthwhile at this time. To tick of your requirements for the year, I need to complete a quick check-in call to go over what you have been doing in your project. Is there a time that suits you for me to give you a call in the next few weeks and complete this phone check in? Talk soon. sent_emails.body: Hi Stuart And Charlotte, Just a quick note - the National Carbon Farming Conference kicks off this week in Albury. Our team will be there across the three days, including Tuesday’s Soil Carbon Day, which we’re co-sponsoring. Matthew Warnken will also be MC’ing parts of the event, and we’ll be involved in a few different sessions and panels throughout the week. If you’re heading along, let me know - we can grab a coffee or catch up for a quick chat about how your project’s going. See you there, Claudia Bryant Claudia Bryant | Customer Success Specialist Phone: +61483969401 Mobile: +61498664218 Email: claudia@agriprove.io: mailto:claudia@agriprove.io On Wednesday, 22 October 2025, 12:48:23 pm +1100, Claudia Bryant wrote: Hi Stuart And Charlotte, Next week at the conference, AgriProve will be running a session (Wednesday 5th Nov) called: Project Ecosystem in Action: The Carbon Farming Value Chain It’s a practical look at how the different parts of the soil carbon value chain work together - from the producer and input suppliers to the technology side and the market. The idea is to show what’s actually happening on the ground and how soil carbon projects turn into real outcomes for producers and the broader market. sent_emails.body: HI Justin, The satellite imagery on the base of the map is essentially a photo from a satellite. I am not sure when it is taken exactly as it differs for different areas, but many have suggested that the photo may be pretty old and doesn't show what it looks like today. Its there to just help you find your bearings on the map. The layer that you see when you click on "soil" in the platform. That is not showing you a satellite reading- it is showing you a carbon estimate based on a soil map of your place. This is just a potential indicator and is not actually measuring the carbon and change in your project over time. That is coming, but we are still building that out at the moment. We will do a satellite review of your project on the 12-month anniversary of your projects baselining (that we will send you when its done) - that will give you a better indicator of how things are going and if we think carbon has been sequestered and would resample. That report is based on a satellite that collects data every day, so we can get a good idea of what's happening. Your projects will be due for that in March next year. sent_emails.subject: Re: AgriProve - On Farm Visit - Monday 20/10 with Claudia Bryant
sent_emails.body: Hi Amanda & Pete, Thanks for your time today. It was lovely to meet you and have a look around the farm. I will pass my notes from today onto Ben. That way we can get everything moving quickly. I checked in about a few things we discussed on farm: 1. The Forest Areas: When a forest area is cleared it needs to have 5 years since the clearing to be eligible for a project. This means that the area near the really scrubby bit in the corner would be best not to include. If you really wanted to 5 years after the clearing you could add it in , but that area would need to be baselined so likely wouldn't be worth it for the small area you'll gain. For the area up the top with thinner pines- that is thin enough that it isn't considered forest, so thinning those out as part of management would be okay ( if its within local NRM rule), but it would just be best to check with us before you do it so we can record it once your project starts. Question: Do you know when the pines were removed from that paddock you one way plowed was? And was it thin like the top or a thicker forest area that was cleared? 2. Selling of the Farm I was wrong about the ACCU's. They are tied to you not the land, so if you wanted to sell the farm you would be able to take your ACCU's with you. If they wanted to continue the project: they would then take over the project, we could change the activities to suit them as it would be different to before baseline, and then any ACCU's on top of what you were already issued would be theirs ( as that is what was gained since they owned it). It's very easy if they take over and it is nice and flexible to be able to farm how they want to after you have left. If they didn't want to continue the project there is 2 paths. 1. IF they are still using the land for farming and are happy for us to still come out and do the sampling every 5 years: we would report that the project was no longer continuing, still sample every 5 years to tick the box needed, but the project would be over in that they wouldn't be doing the activities or be eligible to get ACCU's even if they measured an increase in our regulatory sampling. This means you could take your ACCU's and there would be no consequence to you or them as the project would be theirs - they are just not continuing and are meeting sample requirements to still not void the contract and repayment be needed. 2. If though they were planning to NOT farm it e.g. change the land use to something that isnt farming OR they weren't happy for us to continue with the sampling- this project would need to be revoked which would require a repayment of ACCU's. This would mean repaying not just the 75% you got but also our 25% - as that is our payment and you would have to find the other 25% to pay back the government. I know that sounds dramatic, but they would only have to agree to let us take samples 1 day every 5 years ( no real work for them) for it to go with path 1 in that no repayment was required. Also, you could work this out in the conditions of the sale. E.g. If a company was buying it to change it away from farming or they really were being difficult and wouldn't let us come out for 1 day every 5 years, you could work out in the sale contract who would pay that out. That was a lot of information, so if you need me to clarify anything feel free to give me a call. AgriProve will be there again this year. Our Chair, Matthew Warnken, is helping MC parts of the event, and we’re also co-sponsoring the Soil Carbon Day on the Tuesday. A few of us from the team will be around across the three days, so if you’re attending, it’d be great to catch up for a chat about your project or anything happening on farm. Here’s the link if you’d like to check out the program: https://nationalcarbonfarmingconference.com/: https://nationalcarbonfarmingconference.com/ Hope to see you there, Claudia Bryant Claudia Bryant | Customer Success Specialist Phone: +61483969401 Mobile:+61498664218 Email: claudia@agriprove.io: mailto:claudia@agriprove.io

sent_emails.subject: Carbon Project Updates
sent_emails.body: Good Morning Ian, Sorry that it took me longer to get back to you than expected. I had to chase up a few things for you in addition to just the reviews we spoke about last week. With your Annual Reviews for the past few years - we passed them on to Lawrie Co, so you may have been correct in that you hadn't seen them before. I have attached both 2024 and 2025's Annual Reviews for all of your projects to this email. If you would like I would be happy to explain this better to you on the phone, but basically, we compare what the trend was in the 5 years prior to baseline and compare that to the past years after baseline. If the trend is better than that of the 5 years prior we consider it positive and it is likely worthwhile resampling, If its not as good as the 5 years prior to baseline then we consider it a negative result and we would not be intending to resample at that time. As you will see you do have some projects that have had a positive result in your 2025 reviews. This means that we potentially would like to resample some of your projects this year. The hold-up is we have a new model that I mentioned that we are running everything through and is the ultimate decider on if we will resample. Your projects are on the list to be put through the model, and we will be in touch when we have a result on if and when we would do that. Someone will be in touch, but if you have any further questions feel free to contact me anytime. As you will see in the attached document your projects average NDRE has had a negative trend compared to the baseline period. sent_emails.body: Good Afternoon Maurice, I have just completed the Annual Satellite review of your carbon projects. Each year we complete a review via satellite of your project to see if the NDRE ( Normalized Difference Red Edge) trend on your farm in the past 12 months is indicative of soil carbon sequestration. We compare the recent trend to those of the 5 years prior to baseline sampling. If the average change is higher since baselining- that suggests soil carbon sequestration is likely to have occurred. As you will see in the attached document your projects average NDRE has had a negative trend compared to the baseline period. This means that your project has not met our threshold for us to complete resampling this year. Next year we will review your project again to decide if resampling would be worthwhile. This trend does not mean carbon has gone backwards, it is showing that the trend in vegetation greenness has been lower than your baseline average and therefore it is unlikely re sampling would be worthwhile. To tick of your requirements for the year, I need to complete a quick check-in call to go over what you have been doing in your project. Is there a time that suits you for me to give you a call in the next few weeks? sent_emails.subject: AgriProve Annual Review Result
sent_emails.body: Good Morning Sophie, I have just completed the satellite annual review of your project. The review is based on Normalized Difference Red Edge (NDRE), a dataset obtained from satellite imagery that is used measure, model, and track seasonal changes in chlorophyll concentration. The assessment has shown an increase in NDRE from the baseline to the current period , which suggests resampling the project is likely worthwhile. (Results attached.) sent_emails.subject: Carbon Project LIA Results
sent_emails.body: Good Afternoon Scott, Attached are your satellite annual review results. Each year we complete a review via satellite of your project to see if the NDRE ( Normalized Difference Red Edge) trend on your farm in the past 12 months is indicative of soil carbon sequestration. We compare the recent trend to those of the 5 years prior to baseline sampling. If the average change is higher since baselining- that suggests soil carbon sequestration is likely to have occurred. As you will see in the attached document your 8 projects had a negative trend since baselining. What this means is that your project has not met our threshold for us to complete resampling this year. Next year we will review your project again to decide if resampling would be worthwhile. This trend does not mean carbon has gone backwards, it is showing that the trend in vegetation greenness has been lower than your baseline average and therefore it is unlikely re sampling would be worthwhile. I will give you a call to tick off the implementation part of the review and we will revisit this next year. If you have any questions, feel free to give me a call to discuss this further. sent_emails.subject: Soil Sampling Quotes
sent_emails.body: Good afternoon Robert, Attached is the pricelist from the lab that we do our soil samples. This is an old one but is a good starting point. These are the prices for the lab process and then there would be the additional cost of sampling if you wanted to outsource that. sent_emails.subject: AgriProve Project Information
sent_emails.body: Good Afternoon Frank, Thanks for your time on the phone yesterday. I have checked in on the details that we discussed and here is a summary: * If you would like to continue the project there will be no cost to you. * Will has already covered the original baseline sampling and as a part of our agreements we cover all the sampling after that. * In terms of risk: we take on most of it as we cover the ongoing costs of the project, there is no claim over your land by us or the regulator (government), we let you make the decisions on how you farm, and if there is a decrease in carbon after an increase you don't need to pay anything back for that. * How we get paid is we get a commission of 25% of the ACCU's you generate. If you don't get ACCU's that is OUR loss. * Your involvement is really running your farm in a way that promotes soil carbon, keeping your records for reporting and the occasional review from us. ( a phone call) * In terms of paperwork - we do most of that. All we need from you is the simple farm records you keep already to show what has been done on the land. So If you do want to take it over, once we had done the contract to get this swapped to you its not going to be much additional work. * Every 5 years we do an audit in which the projects get looked at in more detail and the records are bought together. The project on your land is 4 years in, so this would happen next year, but we would handle getting the information for the start off Will and would only need information about what you have done since taking over. We will pull it together and submit it for you based on what you give us. * In terms of your farming practices- because you plant brassica which is a legume, would have changed your stocking rate since you took over and are applying nutrients to address deficiencies: which are all practices good for carbon I think we could find a way for you to continue and be farming in a way that aligns with your preferences. How I see it is this is an opportunity for you to get paid for the carbon you generate on your farm at no cost to you. I know that can seem a little bit too good to be true, but this is how we make it a good deal for farmers which allows us to benefit too. We only get paid from this point if you do too. Below is some more information about us: Our website & map of projects: https://agriprove.io/ Case Studies of our farmers: https://agriprove.io/casestudies Our knowledge hub with FAQ's: https://help.agriprove.io/ Please note that the process would be shorter for you than what you read in the resources as you already have the baseline and all the prep that came with that being done. Your main steps from now are outlined above. Have a look over this and I will touch base next week sometime. If you have questions about the details, please call Dylan on 0401101748. He knows lots about it all. sent_emails.subject: Carbon project Review Due
sent_emails.body: Good Afternoon Lisa, I am getting in touch as your carbon project is due for its Annual Review. This has 2 parts. The first is a satellite assessment of your farms NDRE. This gives us an idea based on the vegetation change on your farm from satellite imagery whether carbon sequestration has been likely to occur. If this result is positive, we will resample your project to get a measurement and see if carbon sequestration has occurred. If it is negative- we will not resample and will reassess next year. The other part of this is we need to do a check-in to record what has been done, check in with you and make sure everything is going as planned. We are currently completing your satellite assessments and would love to get your check-in call done this week as well. Is there a time this week that suits you to go through this? It will take a maximum of 30 minutes and is generally a lot shorter than that. Could you please let me know a time that suits to call you or feel free to call me. sent_emails.subject: Soil carbon project annual remote assessment results
sent_emails.body: Good Morning Robert, I am reaching out to let you know the results of your carbon projects reviews. As part of our process each year we complete a desktop assessment of your projects Normalized Difference Red Edge (NDRE). This is a measurement of seasonal changes in chlorophyll concentration that we get from satellite imagery. We use this as an indicator for the potential for increases in soil organic carbon to have occurred on your project. As you would probably have been expecting with the current seasonal conditions- all 3 of your project areas did not see an increase over the past year. I have attached the reports showing the NDRE change before and since baseline to this email. What this means is that these projects have not met our threshold and we will not be resampling these projects this year. We will do this review again and re- revaluate next year. If you have any questions about this or want to chat about anything around your soil carbon project feel free to reach out. sent_emails.subject: Frazer Carbon Project Review & Resampling Request
sent_emails.body: Good Afternoon Perina, I am getting in touch to update you with the next steps for your Carbon Project. I have just completed the desktop annual review of your project. This is where we assess the Normalized Difference Red Edge (NDRE) change on your property overtime using satellite imagery. We use this as an indicator of potential for increases in soil organic carbon sequestration to have occurred on the project. As you will see in the attached document there has not been a huge change over the period. Normally we would possibly not sample with a small change like this, however your project is in year 5 and re sampling is required to meet our reporting requirements. engagements.subject: RE: Re questions re "Reef Credits"
engagements.body: Hi Jeff, Yes, the platform is basing its assessment of eligibility off geographical location within the reef catchment areas. A Reef Credit project and Soil Carbon sequestration project can co-exist and we are actively targeting those landholders with an existing project with us that may be interested in Reef credits under the Grazing Land Management (GLM) method. I’ll pass your query over to Bill Hyem in our team to look further into this for you. Natural sequence farming seems like it would be a great addition to the property from my limited knowledge on it, and should help reduce fine sediment loss and nutrient runoff. However, there are some points to be aware of to be eligible for a GLM Reef credit project: * one or more additional or new management activities is implemented, * management activities are reasonably expected to improve ground cover for water quality improvement that are beyond what is required by legislation or pre-existing formal obligations, * grazing is the principle land use for the last seven years, and * broad scale clearing of woody vegetation has not occurred within the previous seven years. From the looks of it, if you were to start a reef credit project based purely on implementing natural sequence farming principles the project would go under the “Gully Method” which involves landscape rehabilitation and construction. We may struggle to prove additionality under the Grazing method as it would need to be a new activity relative to what you’re already doing with the carbon project. See attached guidance on Reef credits under the Grazing Land Management Methodology. We’ll get back to you with our thoughts after reviewing the situation further. From: Jeff Bell Sent: Sunday, 2 February 2025 2:55 PM To: Dylan Jones Subject: Re questions re "Reef Credits" Hi Dylan, The Agriprove platform said "Generate income through a Reef Credit project Your property is eligible to undertake a Reef Credit Project." Is this correct or is it just that we are geographically eligible? Can a reef credit project co-exist with a carbon project? I have been looking into "natural sequence farming" which is all about keeping water and dissolved nutrients on farm through modifying existing contour drains and/or constructing level contours.(which fits neatly into what the "reef credit project" would be looking to achieve. Attended a "natural sequence farming" field day yesterday and there was so much that explained why areas of our farm have limited performance compared to the mean. If we spend money on training and earthworks to keep more water and nutrients on our farm(approx 94 % of which is under a carbon project) would we be eligible for a "reef credit project"? Jeff Bell

engagements.subject: Re: Re questions re "Reef Credits"
engagements.body: Hi Dylan, Definitely would not be grazing management as that is already done. It would be remedial earth works to modify the existing drain contours and where needed construct new contours to slow the flow of water and nutrients and keep both on farm rather than running off down the waterway which does come in the list of gully management methodology activities. Most of the farm can benefit from this in productivity(and consequently carbon sequestration) but only about 30 percent of the farm(my guestimate) has substandard ground cover which in my opinion could release some sediment and nutrients off farm. My take is that the amount of sediment lost from the farm in its current condition would be to low to bother with. The only place where there would be any amount would be a bit hard to manage as it comes pouring through from next door in a water way only a couple of hundred metres from our bottom fence. If Agriprove think there is anything worth pursuing then I will think about it. I myself think not but that is an opinion not based on knowledge. From: Dylan Jones Sent: Monday, 3 February 2025 10:11 AM To: Jeff Bell Cc: Bill Hyem Subject: RE: Re questions re "Reef Credits" Hi Jeff, Yes, the platform is basing its assessment of eligibility off geographical location within the reef catchment areas. A Reef Credit project and Soil Carbon sequestration project can co-exist and we are actively targeting those landholders with an existing project with us that may be interested in Reef credits under the Grazing Land Management (GLM) method. I’ll pass your query over to Bill Hyem in our team to look further into this for you. Natural sequence farming seems like it would be a great addition to the property from my limited knowledge on it, and should help reduce fine sediment loss and nutrient runoff. However, there are some points to be aware of to be eligible for a GLM Reef credit project: * one or more additional or new management activities is implemented, * management activities are reasonably expected to improve ground cover for water quality improvement that are beyond what is required by legislation or pre-existing formal obligations, * grazing is the principle land use for the last seven years, and * broad scale clearing of woody vegetation has not occurred within the previous seven years. From the looks of it, if you were to start a reef credit project based purely on implementing natural sequence farming principles the project would go under the “Gully Method” which involves landscape rehabilitation and construction. We may struggle to prove additionality under the Grazing method as it would need to be a new activity relative to what you’re already doing with the carbon project. See attached guidance on Reef credits under the Grazing Land Management Methodology. We’ll get back to you with our thoughts after reviewing the situation further. engagements.subject: Carbon Project- Annual Review Results
engagements.body: Good Afternoon Jeff, I have just completed your yearly satellite assessment for your carbon project. As you know we use this as an indicator for if we think resampling would be worthwhile. Your assessment this year ( attached) has shown an increase in the average NDRE from baseline to current period and an increase in the past year. This indicates that re-sampling this year would be worthwhile. Please note that while NDRE is an indicator there are many other factors that can influence sequestration. This does not guarantee that soil organic carbon has increased. We need to complete the physical sampling to know what is happening in the ground. Next steps: Before we schedule the resampling date, we need to complete the phone call section of the review. Is there a time next week that would suit to do that? I have some prep I need to do before the call so locking in a time in advance works best. If you have any questions please let me know. Talk soon. Kind regards, Claudia Claudia Bryant | Customer Success Specialist [AgriProve] Phone: +61483969401 Mobile: +61 498 664 218 Email: claudia@agriprove.io Address: Level 1, 601 Dean Street Albury NSW 2640 [Lynch CP option 1 (1).png] www.agriprove.io [cid:3d7261ff-c891-4849-ad36-645ab0eda247] [cid:f301fe00-ff21-4b73-9fa2-956a828f9cce] [cid:f2663d93-f230-4c07-be33-d7023d883512] [cid:1be732a4-a6cf-4d4f-9f87-11c9d3beebb2] Here at AgriProve we care for your privacy. engagements.body: Hi Ross, Thank you for your response and noting about the Education section. I have re-worded it as below: "Ross and Dimity attended a course led by Graeme Sait and Nicole Masters, which fundamentally shifted their perspectives and prompted them to alter their farming practices. engagements.subject: Sampling Results - Nox 2024
engagements.body: Hi Ross, Please see attached the results from the last round of sampling completed on the two project areas. In summary: * Chifley Carbon Project is now 650 tC above the baseline carbon stock and has shown a consistent increasing trend since the sampling round completed in early 2023. This means we can go ahead and begin the process of reporting and applying for ACCUs for this project. * Daly Carbon Project is not above the baseline carbon stock to date however this project shows the same consistent increasing trend since the early 2023 sampling, with three of the 4 CEAs continuing to show gains since 2023. Overall I think these are really positive results. With regard to Chifley Carbon Project, before we can estimate the total ACCU yield we will need to do some work to estimate any emissions associated with the project period to feed into our calculations. I have copied Imogen Hickey to this email who is our crediting specialist, it would be great if we can arrange a time to jump on a video call to talk through the process from here and next steps to work toward lodging an application for ACCUs. Feel free to give me a call or otherwise let us know a time that might suit for a brief meeting. From: Ross Thompson Sent: Saturday, 7 June 2025 1:03 PM To: Kieren Whittock Subject: RE: Agriprove form for the CER Hi Kieren, I was wondering if it is possible that we could delay catching up on this until mid Spring? I feel you will have more chance of "cutting through" with me then, when I start heading into our slower time of year (Mid Spring til late Summer). As you know, I am pretty wound up with the CER and their demands and then the fact that "estimates" are OK. I just do not see how I can possibly justify loading up future generations with this burden. But I think, given all the work we have done up til now, I should listen carefully to you, and we should TRY to resolve it and move on. Rather than throwing the baby out with the bath water. No promises that you will be able to swing me around in my attitude. But if you can wait until I am more receptive, I think it gives us the best chance. What are your thoughts? If you are agreeable, have diarised to get in touch with you by email on October 1. I would simply be replying to your email below to get the ball rolling and set aside some time for us to work on it together as you suggested. Regards Ross From: Kieren Whittock > Sent: Friday, 28 March 2025 9:46 PM To: Ross Thompson > Subject: RE: Agriprove form for the CER Hi Ross, So having a look in some more detail here. As discussed we are trying to achieve two things with this information. 1. Show that at least one of the eligible activities has been implemented on the project area 2. Gather the data we need to quantify emissions associated with the project that feed into the calculations Regarding point 1, this is what we are trying to achieve with the Activity Log pages. What is important to note on these activities is that we only need to demonstrate that one of these has occurred, not all of them. As a starting point we could select one that may be the easiest to demonstrate, and only make reference to the others as complimentary activities without being required to demonstrate them in detail or provide detail that is difficult to obtain. From your notes it sounds like this may be achievable. Regarding point 2, if we put aside the stock numbers for the moment, we can strike a few things out from the start. I don't believe irrigation and landscape modification are relevant in your scenario and can be disregarded. That leaves the inputs, which it seems you have some records for, at least for total quantities which we will be able to work with. I also think residues will be able to be resolved given you are primarily a grazing operation and this section is more aimed at cropping operations. Regarding stock numbers, I think it would be worthwhile if we could jump on a quick call with Will at a time that suits you to ask some targeted questions that can help us better determine what can be done. Also, to clarify, the expectation is not for you to fill out the tables provided - we can do this work based on raw information provided, before cross-checking with you that we have interpreted correctly. As discussed, I would be more than happy to come and see you face to face, I could complete as much of this as I can on the fly while there - we have done this a few times previously and has b…

engagements.body: Good Morning Ross, Thanks for sending those details through. We definitely haven't put it in the too hard basket - it just hasn't been an urgent priority up until now as it's coming up to the reporting period date. I will touch base with Kieren and have cc'ed him into this email to see what we can do. In terms of the record keeping - we would never expect you to guess, and it is a lot simpler than it sounds. Most of it is things that you would already have had to collect and would have given to your accountant eg. invoices for expenses such as seed and fertilizer, livestock numbers, fuel used ect. The main thing that the regulator needs is proof that you have changed practices in some way and that you have implemented what you said you would. They don't need extreme detail of every little thing that you have done on farm. If you would find it helpful, I can jump on a call with you and we can look at your map, go through what you've done on your project, what records you have, and put together a bit of a plan/list of what you need to proceed and get this done. It was cropped for three years (zero-till) , then zero-till pasture was re-established. This occurred last year (i.e. FY2024–25), not FY22–23 as previously recorded — Ross confirmed the earlier record was incorrect. Ross noted he hadn't included it in records due to its small size, but Dylan confirmed it should be documented regardless. Eligible Activity — Grazing Management (Main Activity) Start date confirmed: 01/01/2022. Dylan had initially suggested 07/01/2021 but Ross preferred 01/01/2022 as more accurate. Declaration date on file: April 2021. Stocking Rate / Grazing Practice Changes Ross does not manage to a specific LSU or head-per-paddock target. His grazing targets are: Maintain pasture sward at 10 cm minimum at all times Target 100% ground cover Average grazing duration per paddock: ~1 week (5–10 days) Previously, stock were set-stocked for up to 6 weeks — a significant change in grazing intensity/duration At any one time, approximately 90% of the property is rested Next Steps Dylan to finalise the landholder statement document and send to Ross for review Ross to sign page 3 (landholder statement page) Following sign-off, move to audit engagement

engagements.subject: AgriProve - Strategy Call
engagements.body: Hi Katie, Thank you for booking a soil carbon project strategy meeting. This meeting will cover: 1. Select the property boundaries on your soil carbon project. 2. Define the eligible activities you will be implementing on your project. 3. Provide a walkthrough of the Land Management Strategy and the Consent to Register and Commitment to Implement Document (CTR-CTI) 4. Answer any additional questions that you have since our first meeting. We also need to collate historical farm records (5 years), so please have the following information on hand: Lot and plan number for the property General nutrient and mineral applications Any pasture renovation information including species composition and hectares planted each year Approximate yearly livestock stocking rates, Any cropping information (grain, seed, and horticulture) including hectares planted, type, and yield. Need to make changes? Reschedule: https://app.hubspot.com/meetings/daniel-wortmann/agriprove-strategy-call?rescheduleId=bea132b1a32fc029d5f4edd031222ed3&ms=1 Cancel: https://app.hubspot.com/meetings/daniel-wortmann/agriprove-strategy-call?cancelId=bea132b1a32fc029d5f4edd031222ed3&ms=1 ________________________________________________________________________________ Microsoft Teams Need help? engagements.subject: Why Southern Queensland is Australia's carbon capital
engagements.body: G'Day Christophe, Ben from AgriProve here. I wanted to personally reach out because you're farming in what is objectively Australia's most productive region for soil carbon projects and I thought you should know why that matters for your bottom line. Let's talk about the Southern Queensland soil profile: Southern Queensland sits in the sweet spot for ideal soil profiles, resulting in soil carbon sequestration. Vertosols, Dermosols and Chromosol soil types can sequester higher than average carbon stocks that translates directly to potential ACCUs (Australian Carbon Credit Units) per hectare. If your farm is over 400 hectares and you want to chat further, feel free to call me on+61 483 921 562 , or do you have a time this week and would like to book in for a quick chat? See my link below. engagements.body: Good Afternoon Christophe, I have chased up your results and attached them to this email. Sorry that there was such a delay on getting them to you. For future, something to be aware of is all of the results automatically go into our online platform where you can see them in there as soon as they are ready. engagements.subject: Re: {EXTERNAL} Yallamundi HORIZON Report
engagements.body: Hey Piet, I have checked with the tech team. They said the issue is likely that because the proposed areas are currently olive plantations, they are classified in the QLD database as woody vegetation and are automatically excluded from the eligibility areas by our system. (see attached screenshot of the layer). "I have checked with the operations team to check on their eligibility and Will said the below: The olive grove can be considered eligible land as cropping is a land use. Then - in regards to clearing: (2) Woody vegetation may be cleared only if: (a) any clearing is undertaken in accordance with any applicable regional natural resource management plan and Commonwealth, State, Territory or local government environmental and planning laws; and (b) at least one of the following apply: (i) the clearing is to manage woody horticulture crops, as part of standard business operations; (ii) the clearing is required to manage woody horticulture crop, following a disturbance; (iii) the clearing is to manage growth of a known weed species as defined in the CFI Regulations; (iv) the clearing is required to reduce the risk of fire; (v) the land was not forest cover in the 5 years prior to the lodgement of the section 22 application for the project or the section 29 application for the land. So you can clear the woody land, under (2)(a) and 2(b)(i); assuming that we can show the grove was at end or life, or it's standard to clear after x years; and the grove is x years old... Then an eligible activity would be establishing and permanently maintaining pasture and grazing." So that area would likely still be eligible. We can get you a map if you would like, but it will take some time as we will have to manually map it all and it wouldn't be a priority at the moment. Let me know but it may take weeks to a month and if they are planning to proceed with a project, we would do that in the onboarding process. For some quick maths for the decision making it would be the correct area x the predicted ha yield x years. engagements.subject: AgriProve - Project Scoping kick off
engagements.body: Hi Tony, Yolande, Fred and Rita, ​Thank you for taking the time to complete the engagement documents with me. I look forward to getting your project scoping underway. To get started please review, sign and return the Consent to Register - Commitment to Implement forms for Double Valley and Corally Glen. I have also attached our Land Management Strategy that accompanies all AgriProve projects detailing how your project(s) are managed and monitored by AgriProve while ensuring our landholders maintain full management autonomy. A land management strategy is required by the Clean Energy Regulator for all Carbon Projects registered with them. I have also attached the Hone Grant agreement, please return one for each property with the relevant landowners signing. Once returned, you’ll be assigned a dedicated Soil Carbon Project Officer and we will begin our project scoping process by: 1. Verifying your Land titles 2. Defining the soil carbon project area(s) - we will need to exclude areas that we cannot physically sample such as roads, dams, heavily timbered areas and other infrastructure 3. Designing project structure - based on operation type, land characteristics, and soil type. We employ a variety of technologies to do this. Our recommendations aim to maximise project success and ACCU yield. 4. Provide a quote on soil baseline sampling (your only project fee). 5. Provision you with our Sales and Licence Agreement to move forward. Once complete, you’ll have clarity of what’s involved when working with AgriProve on your soil carbon journey. engagements.subject: AgriProve - Process changes impacting projects registered after 8th November
engagements.body: Dear Tony, Yolande, Fred and Rita, I hope this message finds you well. Since our conversation and decision to execute the documentation for the additional projects in the pipeline for Corally Glen, there has been some development with the regulator that I wanted to pass on to keep you informed. The importance of the update is that it may impact your carbon project registration with AgriProve. The Clean Energy Regulator (CER) is updating some of their processes, and as a result, if we do not receive your sign agreement (Key Commercial Terms) by the 8th November we will need to revise your documentation to ensure we align with their requirements. This will mean additional paperwork for you, and we understand how valuable your time is. To avoid any unnecessary delays, we’re aiming to have all current agreements signed and finalised before 8th November. I understand the additional document has only just come through, so I apologies about the quick turn around, but I wanted to do you the curtesy of providing you as much time as possible. As it turns out, the decision to proceed with registration now, but hold off baselining was made at a fortuitous time to avoid this additional paperwork! Please note that as discussed, signing now does not lock you in to baselining immediately. Your projects can be withdrawn up until point of baseline and we will work with you to schedule sampling if you would like to proceed, and at a time that suits you. Invoicing for baselining only occurs after sampling has been completed and results are supplied to you. You will also notice the quote came to $13,000 for the additional projects, not the expected $17,000 which is fantastic. Our priority is making this as seamless as possible for you and ensuring that your project moves forward without extra hassle. We’re here to support you through this process and ensure that everything is handled smoothly and with your best interests in mind. I'll give you a call tomorrow to make sure you received my email and should you have any questions or need assistance, don’t hesitate to reach out. engagements.subject: Carbon Project Annual Review Results
engagements.body: Good Afternoon Tony, I have just completed the Annual Satellite review of your carbon projects. Each year we complete a review via satellite of your project to see if the NDRE ( Normalized Difference Red Edge) trend on your farm in the past 12 months is indicative of soil carbon sequestration. We compare the recent trend to those of the 5 years prior to baseline sampling. If the average change is higher since baselining- that suggests soil carbon sequestration is likely to have occurred. As you will see in the attached document your projects average NDRE has had a negative trend compared to the baseline period. This means that your project has not met our threshold for us to complete resampling this year. Next year we will review your project again to decide if resampling would be worthwhile. Please note this is not a bad thing or indicative of if things are going backwards, it just means that there hasn't been enough positive change yet to justify resampling, which is to be expected as your project is not even 12 months old. To tick of your requirements for the year, I need to complete a quick check-in call to go over what you have been doing in your project. Is there a time that suits you for me to give you a call in the next few weeks? engagements.subject: Tags for Tonnes set-up and next steps
engagements.body: Good morning Karen, Welcome to the Tags for Tonnes team!! We are proud and excited to offer a world-first initiative such as this to assist with your carbon project management. Now that we have your tags on the way, we are progressing to have you set-up and ready by the time your tags arrive. Here is a short guide on how to operationalise your tags when you receive them: 1. The instructions will be on a small welcome card in your package - scan the QR code with your phone camera to access them. 2. Charging the tags in the sun is the first step to getting started (they will need to sit in the sun for 5-7 days to charge fully). 3. I have created an account for you in our software and have uploaded your farm boundaries in it. 4. We will need to jump on a video call so I can run you through how to connect your tags to our software - this will require making a Ceres Tag account in their portal, and registering your tags to our software (I will walk you through this step-by-step) . 5. Once your tags are charged and you are set-up in the software you are ready to tag 6. It is important to record as many details around which animal you are tagging (Ceres tag number, VID, NLIS ID, age) using what tag and what mob/class/breed they belong to. 7. Taking a picture of the animal is also an important step to help tell their story. 8. Once tagged, and the animal data is recorded we can jump on a call to set up your animal information in the 'My Herd' section of the software - this will power all the insights you can get on your herd's performance. 9. You are ready to go! When your tags have arrived, let me know and we can organise our first video call. Any questions you may have please feel free to reach out to me. We are excited to start this new chapter of carbon farming with you! Hi Karen, I hope you are going well! I am filling out the co-benefits report for LRF to unlock the payment. I was wondering if you could please fill gaps and expand on my answers to bold questions below, and provide any additional photos on management activities (grazing, weed control, sowing, fencing). The report is for the period of the 1/11/2022 to 1/11/2023. Weed management - Please provide details on this activity undertaken during the reporting period. Include as much information as possible, including location and size of the area where the activity has occurred, the frequency and in which months, include any planned works that did not take place and reasons why. * Weed management was conducted across the property by both the landholders and contractors. Contractors completed approximately 52 hours of weed management plus additional hours by the landholders. Chemical application was conducted to control highest priority weeds; Cats claw, Giant rats tail grass and Lantana. Chemical weed control was conducted in line with Land Management Report. Did you do any fire management as well? Stock management in remnant areas - Please provide details on this activity undertaken during the reporting period. Include as much information as possible, including location and size of the area where the activity has occurred, the frequency and in which months, include any planned works that did not take place and reasons why. Remnant vegetation areas have been fenced off with X km fence installed and X new troughs. Remnant areas have been carefully grazed according to Land Management Report. Holistic grazing management was implemented providing project areas with sufficient rest periods to enable full recovery of plants and root mass, maximising soil carbon. Grazing has been conducted rotationally for short durations X days, X times per year, allowing X rest. Grazing is conducted based on feed availability to reduce impact on native trees and shrubs. Stock are removed so there is always 100% groundcover remaining. Smaller areas are fenced off using electric tape to enable rotational grazing. Currently paddock sizes are 100ha but we are looking to reduce this using (electric) tape to avoid grazing too heavily’. Stock management in riparian areas - Please provide details on this activity undertaken during the reporting period. Include as much information as possible, including location and size of the area where the activity has occurred, the frequency and in which months, include any planned works that did not take place and reasons why. XX km of waterways and riparian zones on the property have been fenced off to keep stock out and to rehabilitate waterways, to slow water and prevent erosion and runoff. Fencing of all riparian corridors X km fencing with X troughs installed. Grazing has been conducted according to Land Management Report. Grazing has only been conducted in riparian zones as crash grazing/short duration grazing once per year. Grazing density is determined based on feed availability. Stock are removed so that there is always 100% groundcover remaining to avoid bare ground and erosion. Grazing has only been conducted in riparian zones when conditions are dry. Photos: Do you have any photos of: -Weed management -Stock restriction/grazing in remnant or riparian zones? -photos of the work or work done by the man you hired? -Any other photos of work completed (eg fencing/water). Thankyou! Melanie

engagements.body: Hi Karen, It was lovely speaking to you yesterday and learning more about your operation. I have written a draft of what we would like to post in the AgriProve Carbon Builders group on Facebook, I will pop it down below in this email. If you could give it a read and send back if you have any concerns or thoughts with it that would be amazing please. We are happy to alter and change things if you are not comfortable sharing certain pieces of information. We would also love to tag you in the post as well, is this something you would be comfortable with? Here is the draft: "Afternoon Carbon Builders! This week we have an insight to another one of our members, Karen Scanlan from Kenmay Station. She spoke in an interview to the changes made in management and the most prominent results observed. Bio and carbon project: Karen and her husband Robert run a cattle operation in the Gladstone region of Queensland and have been involved in a carbon project since 2020. Their main motivations for starting a carbon project were to improve the environment and increase both flora and fauna diversity to integrate wildlife with cattle. Natural capital: In conjunction with their soil carbon project, they have an Accounting for Nature project that measures natural capital (co-benefits). The improvements to management have been measured, packaged and sold to the Queensland Government through the Land Restoration Fund. See more about their project here: https://www.accountingfornature.org/auacc56 Previous management: Through strategic management and infrastructure development they have been able to transform the property from being run down due to set stocking and lack of active management to a thriving landscape. Management conversion: They have made considerable improvements to the property in terms of fencing infrastructure with internal fences and laneways to assist with rotational grazing. They now are able to run 320 head of cattle through nine paddocks to allow for pasture rejuvenation. Multi-species perennial pastures have been sowed to increase biodiversity and biomass to reduce run off into the Great Barrier Reef. Their future plans are to further develop their fencing infrastructure to extend the rest periods and continue to improve pastures. Results: As a result, they have been able to quadruple their carrying capacity and have an increased body of pasture in height and species diversity. Education: Karen has utilised several educational courses and personal experience to create the current and future management plans. Some of these courses were Holistic Management, pasture improvement, and cattle trading, with the greatest influence being Joel Salatin's enterprise stacking method." Thank you so much for you time and looking forward to hearing from you!
